title: Radiology Groups Join Coalition Against $103,265 H-1B Fee on Physicians
excerpt: The American College of Radiology and dozens of physician and patient advocacy groups told federal immigration officials the proposed fee would make it harder to recruit doctors for rural and underserved communities.
body:
• The American College of Radiology joined dozens of physician and patient advocacy organizations in a letter to the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services opposing a proposed $103,265 fee on certain H-1B visa petitions.
  • The coalition warned the fee would make it harder for hospitals, physician practices and other healthcare employers to recruit international physicians, particularly in rural and underserved communities.
  • What it costs: the proposed $103,265 would stack on top of roughly $5,000 in existing H-1B filing charges — alongside the administration's separate $100,000 H-1B fee, imposed by proclamation in September 2025 and currently blocked by courts. The groups want physicians, dentists and medical trainees fully exempted.
  • International medical graduates make up nearly one-quarter of the U.S. physician workforce; the coalition says the fee is already causing employers to pause or abandon recruitment of foreign doctors.

The American College of Radiology has joined dozens of physician and patient advocacy organizations in a letter to the Department of Homeland Security and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services opposing a proposed rule that would impose a new $103,265 fee on certain H-1B visa petitions.

The coalition warned that the fee could make it harder for hospitals, physician practices and other healthcare employers to recruit international physicians, particularly in rural and underserved communities already facing doctor shortages.

In the letter, the organizations noted that international medical graduates make up nearly one-quarter of the U.S. physician workforce and play a critical role in communities facing physician shortages. They argued that additional immigration-related costs and administrative barriers could further strain the healthcare workforce and reduce patient access to care.

The groups urged the agencies to recognize physicians, dentists and medical trainees as serving a permanent national medical interest, exempt them from H-1B-related fees and restrictions, and continue efforts to streamline visa processing.

The fee fight, so far

The White House introduced the six-figure charge in September 2025, when a presidential proclamation set a $100,000 fee on H-1B petitions, saying the program had been exploited to replace American workers with lower-paid labor. Federal courts later blocked collection of the fee, and the administration has extended the measure into 2027 even as the legal battle continues.

Radiology groups began pushing back within days. In a September 2025 letter to Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, the ACR, the Society of Interventional Radiology, the American Medical Association and more than 50 other organizations urged the administration to issue guidance recognizing physician entry as in the national interest — and therefore exempt from the fee.

The campaign then moved to Congress. In mid-March, lawmakers introduced the bipartisan H-1Bs for Physicians and the Healthcare Workforce Act, which would exempt physicians and nurses from the fee and bar the administration from imposing new immigration visa fees beyond those already in U.S. code. The bill's co-sponsors include Reps. Mike Lawler, Maria Elvira Salazar, Sanford Bishop and Yvette Clarke. On April 15, the ACR, the American Society of Neuroradiology and more than 40 other organizations wrote to lawmakers backing the measure.

Why hospitals say the math doesn't work

"The consequences of this fee, and lack of exemptions, are already being felt."

— ACR and more than 40 medical organizations, in a letter to lawmakers

"The added cost is causing health employers, including safety-net hospitals and other practices, to pause or abandon recruitment of physicians and other providers, recruitment that in many cases has been in progress for over a year," the organizations wrote.

The signatories — including the American Medical Association, the American College of Cardiology and the American Society of Anesthesiologists — contend that employers, and especially independent physician groups operating on what they describe as "razor thin margins," cannot absorb a six-figure fee on top of existing onboarding costs. The result, they say: longer wait times, deferred care and more pressure on emergency departments that are already overburdened.

"Without these providers, many communities would have little to no access to the care patients depend on, and the fee is now actively undermining the pipeline that delivers them," the groups wrote, calling the exemption bill "a narrowly tailored, commonsense solution" aimed at keeping physicians and essential healthcare workers out of a fee structure they say was designed for other sectors.

The diaspora dimension

For the Indian diaspora, the dispute has a direct edge. Indian professionals are among the largest groups of H-1B visa holders in the United States, and Indian-trained physicians form a significant share of the international medical graduates who, by the coalition's own figures, make up about one in four practicing American doctors — disproportionately serving rural and underserved areas.

A $103,265 per-petition fee changes the hiring calculus for the hospitals and practices that employ them. Safety-net hospitals and independent practices — the facilities most likely to recruit international physicians — are also the employers least able to absorb six-figure costs, which is why the coalition argues the fee lands hardest exactly where shortages are worst.

What happens next

The proposed rule now moves through the federal rulemaking process, where the coalition's letter is part of a growing record of opposition from the medical establishment. The bipartisan exemption bill remains before Congress, and the courts are still weighing the legality of the original $100,000 proclamation fee — a fight that now turns on Congress's authority over immigration fees.

For hospitals weighing whether to sponsor an international physician, the practical question is timing: whether an exemption for healthcare workers arrives before the fee takes effect. The coalition's message to DHS and USCIS is that the recruitment pipeline is already freezing up — and that the cost will show up in waiting rooms, not just budgets.
image_caption: An MRI scanner in a hospital radiology suite. Radiology groups are urging the Trump administration to exempt physicians from the new $100,000 H-1B fee.
nri_angle: The fee would hit hardest at safety-net hospitals and rural practices that rely on international medical graduates, a workforce that includes many Indian-trained physicians working in the US on H-1B status.
